content: The Poison Control Center (PCC), also known as the Poison Information Center (PIC), is a specialized medical facility that provides immediate, free, and expert advice and assistance over the telephone in cases of exposure to poisonous or hazardous substances. These centers are equipped to handle inquiries about potential poisons and offer treatment management advice for exposures involving personal care products, household items, medications, pesticides, plants, bites and stings, food poisoning, alcohol, gases, and fumes. Remarkably, over 75% of poison exposure cases are managed solely via telephone, significantly reducing the need for costly emergency room visits or physician consultations. In most countries, poison control centers operate toll-free, 24 hours a day, 7 days a week, and 365 days a year. After World War II, the introduction of numerous new drugs and chemicals into the marketplace led to a sharp increase in both suicide attempts and childhood poisonings. At that time, poisonings accounted for nearly half of all accidental injuries in children, with a significant number resulting in fatalities. These alarming trends prompted the medical community to develop a systematic response to both unintentional and intentional poisonings. In Europe during the late 1940s, specialized toxicology wards were established, with initial facilities in Copenhagen and Budapest. The Netherlands also initiated a poison information service. In the United States, the first poison information center was established in Chicago in 1953. By 1957, there were 17 poison control centers in the U.S., modeled after the Chicago center. These centers primarily addressed physician inquiries, providing information on product ingredients, toxicity, and treatment recommendations. Over time, poison control centers began to accept calls from the general public. Most of these centers were not part of patient treatment facilities but instead focused on providing information. In 1958, the American Association of Poison Control Centers (AAPCC) was founded to foster collaboration among poison centers in different cities and to standardize their operations. The AAPCC also initiated poison prevention and education programs for both healthcare professionals and the general public. In 1968, the American Academy of Clinical Toxicologists (AACT) was established by a group of medical doctors to apply toxicology principles to patient care and improve the national standard of care. During the 1960s and 1970s, the number of poison centers in the U.S. grew rapidly, reaching 661 centers by 1978. However, this trend reversed in the 1980s and 1990s, with many centers closing or merging. By 2000, there were 51 certified centers in the U.S. In Europe, a similar movement occurred, but unlike the American model, most European centers were centralized toxicology treatment facilities integrated with poison information services. France developed inpatient units for treating poisoned patients in the late 1950s. In England, the National Poison Information Service was established at Guy's Hospital under Dr. Roy Goulding, while Dr. Henry Mathew founded a poison treatment center in Edinburgh. In 1964, the European Association for Poison Control Centers was formed in Tours, France. Poison control centers were also established in Australasia during the 1960s. Today, in the United States, the American Association of Poison Control Centers manages a 24-hour hotline staffed by pharmacists, physicians, nurses, and poison information specialists who have received specialized training in toxicology. The hotline also includes a TTY/TDD number for individuals with hearing impairments. Poison educators across the country provide poison prevention training and educational sessions to community institutions, along with distributing educational materials. The national phone number, 1-800-222-1222, routes calls to the nearest local facility. Globally, most countries have poison control centers staffed similarly to those in the United States, ensuring consistent and expert care for poison-related emergencies.
